name: fold-rehearsal
topic: the person's own HARNESS-002R prompt: how carved drapery differs across four sculptures
why_this_fixture: This is the prompt the 002R rehearsal actually failed on, frozen as MODEL OUTPUT rather than
as production logic. It is here because the person's own note already performed the
intelligence the pipeline is supposed to perform — separating a quality from the effect it
produces, tracing each to what was said, and keeping what measurement will not reach — and a
fixture that did less would not test the repair.
NOTHING HERE IS ASSERTED TRUE. Every atom is a frozen model's proposal about what a source unit
says. The fixture proves the SHAPE survives the pipeline, not that any reading is correct.

prompt: even folding through the statues can have different styles the way they affect the perception and make us view the statue. the the buddha statue it feels so metallic somehow very blunt, very sharp edges of the folds, whereas in the woman whose face is covered with the the created fold, that is a damn different art, the artist has carved the fold in such a manner that it creates the effect of transparency--a bit similar is of the dead bed man the folds on his chest are somewhat looking similar but yeah share slight bluntness with buddha--folds in the modern woman sculptures have their own style

images.title: A recumbent figure, seen from the side

theorist_payload.reading: Four carved figures, each resolving cloth differently, and the difference is legible in the edges rather than in the subject.

blocks.text: the seated figure's drapery breaks into facets that meet at abrupt edges
the standing figure's face is covered by a carved veil whose weave is cut through
on the recumbent figure the cloth gathers across the chest in long parallel troughs
the seated and recumbent figures share an abruptness at the edge that the veiled figure does not
the veil reads as thin cloth while remaining continuous stone, and the two readings do not resolve
carving cloth to read as translucent is associated with a nineteenth-century workshop practice
the modern figure's cloth may be resolving into fewer, larger planes than any of the other three
